studyMetadata.title: STOP&SCAN Expert Panel
studyMetadata.description: Structured expert evaluation of STOP&SCAN, a framework for evaluating potentially synthetic media. Participants critique team-authored evaluations of four public cases and compare against SIFT / detector workflows.

uiConfig.studyEndMsg: Thank you for completing the STOP&SCAN expert panel. You may close this window.

consent.instruction: Please read the consent document, then confirm the statements in the sidebar.

response.prompt: I have read this document and have had the chance to ask questions.
I understand that participation is voluntary, that I may skip any question, and that I may stop at any time without giving a reason.
I understand that my responses will be recorded under a code, that interaction timestamps within the study page will be logged, and that de-identified quotations may be published.
I understand that once I submit a response within the study I will not be able to edit it.
I am 18 years of age or older.
(Participants in the EEA, UK, or Switzerland) I explicitly consent to my data being processed as described and transferred to the United States.
I consent to take part in this study.

ratings-stopscan.instruction: Rate STOP&SCAN on the items in the sidebar.

response.prompt: Interaction log
The sequence is clear enough for a non-expert to follow unaided.
Why? (optional)
The five elements are the right five; nothing essential is missing.
Why? (optional)
The distinction between counting evidence channels and counting completed steps is meaningful in practice.
Why? (optional)
Requiring two converging independent channels before a resolved outcome is the right threshold.
Why? (optional)
A non-expert could reliably judge whether two evidence channels are independent.
Why? (optional)
A non-expert could reliably apply the rule that conflicting techniques inside one channel mean that channel returned nothing, rather than balanced evidence.
Why? (optional)
"Withhold judgment" is a realistic outcome that people would actually accept.
Why? (optional)
The framework handles wrongly-dismissed authentic content as well as it handles fabricated content.
Why? (optional)

ratings-sift.instruction: Rate SIFT on the items in the sidebar (before our stated critiques).

response.prompt: Interaction log
SIFT remains adequate for evaluating claims that arrive as synthetic or manipulated media.
Why? (optional)
SIFT’s freedom to stop after one move is appropriate rather than a weakness.
Why? (optional)
Lateral reading reliably improves a judgment in today’s search environment.
Why? (optional)
SIFT gives adequate guidance when the source is authentic but the content is not.
Why? (optional)
SIFT gives adequate guidance when authentic content is wrongly alleged to be synthetic.
Why? (optional)
Caulfield’s AI-specific extension addresses the case where the artifact under evaluation is itself suspected of being AI-generated.
Why? (optional)

ratings-open.instruction: Optional open critique before we state our positions on SIFT.

response.prompt: Interaction log
Where do you expect STOP&SCAN to fail first in real use?
Which STOP&SCAN element is weakest, and what would you change about it?
Requiring every element to be visited — no early exit even when one step seems to settle the matter — is a deliberate choice. Is it the right one?
What, if anything, does STOP&SCAN add that SIFT or lateral reading already covers adequately?
What would you need to see before recommending STOP&SCAN to a non-expert audience?
Is there a framework, practice, or step from your own work that neither of these captures?
Were the evaluations we showed you a fair demonstration of the framework? Did they flatter it, or undersell it?
